name: Deep royal blue
lede: Deep royal blue is exactly what its name describes: a darker-than-usual variant of [[royal-blue|royal blue]], built by the same "intensity plus base color" grammar as most of ColorHub's modifier names.

sections.title: A modifier, not a new color
sections.body:
ColorHub's graph files Deep royal blue as a grammatical modifier of [[royal-blue]], its listed parent, the same pattern that produces names like Vivid royal blue or Dark royal blue from a single base hue [1]. The hex #002366 measures a deep purplish blue by ISCC-NBS, 5.5 units from its nearest block, close to 6.2PB 1.6/9.6 in Munsell notation [2]. Its lightness sits at only 16 out of 100, markedly darker than the brighter royal blue most people picture, which is the entire point of the "deep" modifier [2]. The nearest related name our library carries for this family is *Vivid navy*, listed alongside it as a web variant [1].

Names built this way rarely carry their own coinage story; "deep" plus a base color is a descriptive label anyone could apply, so no single origin date or namer is recorded in the sources we checked [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a close match to Deep royal blue in 14 of 23,781 paintings, 0.06 percent, with the within-painting test narrowing that to 8, making it rarer than about 70 percent of the named colors we track [3]. The earliest match, as photographed, dates to 1644, and inside the paintings that carry it the color plays an accent 88 percent of the time rather than a shadow or a base tone, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. In printed English the phrase rises fastest in the 1920s and peaks in the 2010s, a pattern typical of a descriptive compound that drifts in and out of fashion rather than one tied to a single historical event [4].
